source.title: Junior School Curriculum Design — Arabic Grade 8 (First published 2023, Revised 2024)
source.url: User-supplied local file (Arabic-Grade-8-Design-Formatted-April-2024.pdf); no confirmed public mirror was found during sourcing — see notes.
source.notes: FULLY RESOLVED (2026-08-14): earlier in this sourcing session, a teacher.co.ke mirror (2022 first-published, DRAFT-watermarked, Foreword signed by then-CS Prof. George Magoha) was used and later flagged as likely stale. The user then supplied a screenshot of the official 'SUMMARY OF STRANDS AND SUB-STRANDS' table, which showed a structure with no apparent overlap with the old mirror or with French/German/Mandarin's shared theme pattern — appearing to be a third, distinct architecture. That reading was WRONG. The user subsequently supplied the complete source PDF directly ('Arabic-Grade-8-Design-Formatted-April-2024.pdf', read in full verbatim via the Read tool, native text extraction, not summarized). Its cover reads 'JUNIOR SCHOOL CURRICULUM DESIGN / ARABIC / GRADE 8', 'First published 2023 / Revised 2024', ISBN 978-9914-43-809-3, Foreword signed by the current CS Hon. Ezekiel Ombaki Machogu — confirming this really is the current document. Reading the full body (not just the one-page summary table) revealed that Arabic Grade 8 in fact follows EXACTLY THE SAME architecture as French/German/Mandarin Grade 8: 3 strands (1.0 Listening and Speaking, 2.0 Reading, 3.0 Writing), each built around the SAME 9 shared real-world themes (Greetings and Introduction, Family, My Surrounding, Time, Fun and Enjoyment, Food and Drinks, My Body, Weather and Environment, Getting Around) for 27 numbered sub-strands total (1.1-1.9, 2.1-2.9, 3.1-3.9), each 2 sessions/lessons = 54 lessons, PLUS a standalone 'Showcasing of skills and concepts (Exhibition)' allocation of 6 lessons (tied to the Community Service Learning project in Appendix 1, not assigned to any of the 3 strands) = 60 lessons total. The confusion in the prior pass arose because the one-page 'SUMMARY OF STRANDS AND SUBSTRANDS' table (p.x) AGGREGATES BY SUB-STRAND NAME rather than listing all 27 theme-based entries individually — e.g. 'Phonological awareness' appears at codes 1.2 (Family), 1.7 (My Body, titled 'Phonological awareness: Pronunciation'), and 1.9 (Getting Around, titled 'Phonological Awareness: Pronunciation'), summing to the table's '6' lessons; 'Imitative Speaking' appears at 1.3 and 1.8 summing to '4'; under Reading, 'Reading Fluency' appears at 2.1 and 2.4 (sum 4), 'Reading Aloud' at 2.2 and 2.5 (sum 4), 'Reading Comprehension' at 2.3, 2.6, 2.8 and 2.9 (sum 8), 'Extensive Reading' only at 2.7 (2); under Writing, 'Creative Writing' appears at 3.7 and 3.9 (sum 4) while all other Writing sub-strand names appear once each (2 lessons). All 27 sub-strands below are recorded individually with their own code, name, theme, specific learning outcomes, and key inquiry question(s), transcribed verbatim from the document body (pages 1-56), matching the code/name/theme/specificLearningOutcomes/keyInquiryQuestions shape used for French/German/Mandarin Grade 8. Suggested learning experiences, core competencies, values, PCIs, and links to other learning areas were present in the source but are not transcribed here, consistent with how French/German/Mandarin Grade 8 are recorded in this project. Assessment rubrics (pp.19-20, 39, 57) were reviewed but are not transcribed, again for consistency with sibling files. Appendix 2 (p.60-62) inconsistently retains an old '4.0 Language structures' resources/assessment row that does not correspond to any strand actually present in this document's body or Table of Contents (which lists only Strands 1.0-3.0) — this appears to be a leftover artifact from the prior (now-superseded) draft's 4-strand structure and was NOT used to fabricate a fourth strand here.

essenceNote: Kenya is part of the international community and therefore the learners shall be given an opportunity to learn foreign languages in addition to the national, official and indigenous languages. These foreign languages include: Arabic, French, German and Mandarin. The Learner is expected to acquire the four language skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing at a basic level in the curriculum. This will give the learner an opportunity to acquire language competencies in an experiential, innovative and flexible ways. Foreign languages learning at this level is guided by social-constructivism and environmental theories. Learning of these languages will promote international consciousness and appreciation of one's own and others' cultures. The learner will transit to Senior School having acquired basic proficiency equivalent to A1/YCT2 (verbatim essence statement, identical wording to French/German/Mandarin Grade 8's essence statements).

generalLearningOutcomes.scope: By the end of Junior School (i.e. across Grades 7-9 combined, not Grade 8 alone)
generalLearningOutcomes.notes: Verbatim from the source document's 'GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR ARABIC LANGUAGE' section (p.ix), a document-wide summary preceding the strand tables. Recorded here for reference; not used directly to generate Grade-8-specific quiz content since these outcomes span the full Junior School cycle.
outcomes: Listen and respond appropriately to relevant information in the Arabic language.
Read a wide variety of texts fluently and accurately for lifelong learning.
Write texts legibly, coherently and creatively in the Arabic language.
Express themselves fluently and confidently in varied contexts.
Appreciate the role of Arabic language as a means of embracing creativity and international relevance.
Enjoy communicating in the Arabic language.
Appreciate cultural awareness and exposure to the Arabic language.

subStrands.name: Showcasing of skills and concepts (Exhibition)
subStrands.notes: Allocated 6 lessons. Not one of the 27 theme-based sub-strands above — this is a standalone allocation tied to the Community Service Learning (CSL) project described in Appendix 1 of the source document (a class-wide integrated project run across the 3 terms, involving problem identification, designing a solution, planning, implementation, showcasing/exhibition and reflection). No specific learning outcomes or key inquiry questions are attached to it in the source; it is assessed formatively across its 6 milestones instead.
